problem: The answer says English 'pin' and 'spin' differ in the following vowel. They do not: both have the same vowel /ɪ/ ([pʰɪn] and [spɪn]). The claim is false and a student would carry away a wrong test for phonemicity.
fix: English [pʰ] and [p] never stand in the same environment: [pʰ] occurs word-initially or at the start of a stressed syllable, [p] after /s/. 'pin' [pʰɪn] and 'spin' [spɪn] differ in position (and in the preceding /s/), not in the vowel, so the two sounds never contrast and are allophones of one phoneme /p/. In Hindi, क and ख can stand in the same position (कल / खल) and the meaning changes, so /k/ and /kʰ/ are separate phonemes.

problem: Retroflex is described as curling the tongue tip back 'to the hard palate', which is the same place given for palatal in the next-but-one line. Students will not see how ट and ட differ from /j/.
fix: Retroflex: the tongue tip is curled back so that it touches (or the underside faces) the alveolar ridge and the region just behind it — Hindi ट /ʈ/, Tamil ட. Reserve 'hard palate' for the palatal place, where the tongue body (not the tip) makes the constriction.

problem: 'Tongue blade near the hard palate' is too vague and overlaps with the palatal description, so /ʃ/ and /j/ look like the same place.
fix: Palato-alveolar: the tongue blade makes the narrowing just behind the alveolar ridge, on the way to the hard palate — /ʃ/ in 'ship', /tʃ/ in 'church'. For palatal, the front of the tongue body rises to the hard palate itself — /j/ in 'yes'.

problem: The nucleus is written /i/, but the vowel of 'speaks' is long, /iː/. The short /i/ is a different (though near) vowel and the symbol is wrong.
fix: In 'speaks' /spiːks/, /s p/ is the onset, /iː/ the nucleus, /k s/ the coda.
